reply_text:
Fast-forwarding master to the branch, then looking for the semilattice exemplar cascades.Master is fast-forwarded to `f7ba3a34`. Running the branch's own tests in a separate process (not the shared JVM).Tests pass: 33 tests, 65 assertions. The equation grammar only takes two operands (`a and b`), so a pattern with several prerequisites needs chained helper variables. Writing the probe now.㊥ (result) The branch is on master, and I ran it against the semilattice exemplar, `cascade-three-relations-sample-v1.edn`, which has six peripheral patterns. Read as joined small causal models, it gives results the cascade can't produce on its own:
- **Support and precedence together.** Each order joins cleanly by itself, but joining both is refused as a cycle between ground control and reload. That is exactly the exemplar's own control case, "support is not precedence", produced by the join rather than written down by hand.
- **The declared meets** match "the units both sides depend on", not the meet in the order.
- **A made-up edge** joins without complaint, but it removes four of the five testable predictions.

㊢ (what I did)
- Fast-forwarded futon3c master to `f7ba3a34`. The branch's tests pass: 33 tests, 65 assertions, run in a separate process.
- Wrote the probe `holes/labs/M-diagramprover/cascade_glue_probe.clj` (commit `49ed39cb`). Run it with `clojure -M holes/labs/M-diagramprover/cascade_glue_probe.clj`.
- Each pattern becomes one small model that owns its unit: "unit X holds if pattern X was applied and its prerequisites hold".
- The shared JVM hasn't loaded the new namespaces. They only matter there once something live calls them.

㊢ (findings, in more detail)
1. **Cycle refusal.** Reload supports ground control, but ground control has to come before reload. Joining the two orders therefore gives `:cycle` on ground and reload. The two relations have to stay as two models of the same patterns; merging them into one model doesn't work.
2. **Meets.** For both declared overlaps (ground/heartbeat meeting at event, envelope/reload meeting at seam), the declared meet is exactly what both sides depend on, excluding the pair themselves. That is Alexander's overlap. In the order itself, though, heartbeat sits below ground and reload sits below envelope, so the order-theoretic meet is heartbeat and reload. In this exemplar, "meet" means the shared dependency, not the lattice meet. That's worth stating wherever the semilattice claim is made.
3. **Knock-outs.** These are counterfactuals of the form "had pattern P not been applied, what fails?", and the two readings give different answers:
   - Under precedence, dropping seam fails everything, and reload depends on all five other patterns.
   - Under support, dropping event fails envelope, ground and heartbeat but not reload.
   
   The WM's current feedback has no per-pattern answer of this kind.
4. **Unwarranted edge.** The exemplar's other control adds heartbeat→envelope without evidence. The join accepts it, so the causal reading doesn't catch it. What it does show is the cost: implied independencies among the units drop from 5 to 1. Those are the predictions that evidence could have tested, so false certainty shows up as lost predictions.

㊟ (limits)
- The equation grammar takes only two operands, so I chained helper variables for patterns with several prerequisites.
- Two producers of one token didn't come up here, because every unit has a single owner. Real cascades will need the OR rule.
- Predictions are counted with conditioning on at most one variable, so the count is truncated.
- Values are true/false only. Nothing here touches G.
- I haven't run it on the peripheral sensitivity exemplar. Its cascade graphs are only in Lean (`PeripheralCascadePolicies.lean`), not in EDN.

㊭ (next) The step from here to the War Machine is the run I offered last time: one recorded click's R6 interpretations, joined the same way, with the OR rule added. That would test whether the fit holds on real cascades and not only on hand-written ones.

previous_reply_acts.text:
(where it doesn't fit yet)
1. **Two producers of one token.** In a cascade, several patterns can produce the same token, and the WM simply takes the union. `glue` refuses that as `:double-mechanism`. A cascade version would make each token the OR of its producers' firings. That is a small, deliberate change, but it is a change.
2. **Time and repetition.** A cascade is a rollout over steps, and tokens accumulate. A causal DAG has no cycles and is fixed. Patterns that feed each other would have to be unrolled per step, or `glue` refuses with `:cycle`.
3. **Probability.** The WM scores cascades with rates, posteriors and G. The branch's models are true/false only. Probabilistic mechanisms are the next tier up in M-diagramprover (D3), registered but not built. For structure and counterfactuals, true/false is enough. For anything that feeds G, it isn't.

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-17
previous_reply_acts.text: (the giant connected cascade) PROOF-2a-PLAN records your why/how split: outcome wants are `:role :why` and lifecycle exits are `:role :how`. It also records that these terms are kept so they can link to the cascade you're building in M-象-2000, with no link built yet. Patterns as causal models would supply that link: the why/how tokens become the shared names the pieces join on. A large model made of small ones is exactly what `glue` produces, and it refuses with a reason when the pieces don't fit.
